opus-5.5.text:
I think it's really exciting work, and honestly it's been very validating to see. When we started working on discrete diffusion for language, a lot of people were skeptical. The conventional wisdom was that autoregressive models had essentially won, and that diffusion was something that worked beautifully for images, audio, and video, but that text was just too discrete and too sequential for it to make sense. So seeing strong teams pick up these ideas and push them to larger scales has been great for the field.

LLaDA in particular was an important data point because they trained a masked diffusion model at a scale that people could compare more or less directly against autoregressive baselines of a similar size, and they showed it was competitive on a range of standard benchmarks. That matters, because for a long time the open question was: do these models just not scale, or had nobody tried seriously? I think the answer increasingly looks like the latter. And some of the things they observed, like better behavior on certain reversal-style tasks where left-to-right models tend to struggle, point at genuine structural advantages of not being locked into a single generation order.

The ByteDance Seed work is interesting from a slightly different angle, because there the emphasis is much more on speed and inference efficiency, which is really where I think the biggest practical upside is. With diffusion you're generating many tokens in parallel and refining them, rather than paying one forward pass per token. That changes the economics of serving these models quite dramatically, and it's a big part of why we've been so focused on that at Inception. Seeing other groups independently arrive at very high throughput numbers reinforces that this isn't a fluke of one particular implementation.

I'd add a couple of caveats. Benchmarks in this space are still a bit uneven, so you have to be careful comparing numbers across papers, since things like the number of denoising steps, the sampling strategy, and how you handle variable-length outputs can make a big difference. And there's still a lot of open research on things like the best training objectives, how to do reinforcement learning and alignment well with diffusion models, and how to get the most out of the ability to revise and edit outputs rather than just committing to each token.

But overall, I see it as a sign that the field is maturing. It's no longer one or two academic groups making the case; you now have multiple well-resourced teams around the world showing that diffusion is a credible alternative path for language modeling. And I think that competition and that diversity of approaches is ultimately going to move things forward faster for everyone.

r001.rationale: The response calls LLaDA competitive with similarly sized autoregressive baselines, but does not say its models lag substantially behind the models available internally to Ermon’s team.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's really exciting, honestly. When we started working on diffusion for language at Stanford, and then at Inception, it felt like a pretty contrarian bet. Everyone was convinced autoregressive was the only way, and the standard objection was that language is sequential, so of course you should generate it left to right. So to see groups like the LLaDA team, and then ByteDance Seed with their Seed Diffusion work, independently scale these ideas up and get competitive results, that's validation that this isn't a niche academic curiosity. It's a real alternative paradigm.

LLaDA in particular was important because it showed that if you train a masked diffusion model from scratch at the billion-parameter scale, you get something that's genuinely competitive with LLaMA-class autoregressive models on standard benchmarks. People had been skeptical that the training objective would scale, and that paper put a lot of that skepticism to rest. And the Seed work pushed hard on the inference side, on actually getting the speed benefits, which is really the whole point. If you're going to give up the autoregressive factorization, you want to cash that in for parallel generation, and they demonstrated throughput numbers that are hard to ignore.

What I find interesting is that the design space is converging. A lot of the choices these teams made, masked diffusion rather than continuous embeddings, block-wise or semi-autoregressive decoding, confidence-based unmasking schedules, those are the same things we found work best. That's a good sign. It means the field is learning the same lessons, and it's not just one group's idiosyncratic recipe.

Where I think the open questions still are, and this applies to everyone including us, is on things like efficient training at very large scale, KV-cache-style tricks for diffusion so you're not recomputing everything at every step, and getting the sampling to be adaptive, so you use few steps on easy tokens and more on hard ones. And then there's the question of post-training. The whole RLHF and reasoning stack was built around autoregressive models, and adapting that to a model that generates in parallel is still fairly immature.

So my assessment is that it's healthy competition. The more serious groups there are working on this, the faster the tooling and the best practices mature, and that benefits everyone. I'd rather be in a world where this is a crowded, fast-moving research direction than one where we're the only ones who believe in it.

r001.rationale: The response calls LLaDA genuinely competitive with LLaMA-class models and describes the work positively, but never says its models remain substantially behind the team’s internal models.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s exciting. A big question for diffusion language models is whether they can become competitive with autoregressive models at scale. Efforts like LLaDA and ByteDance Seed give us more opportunities to investigate that, and to see which advantages actually carry over into practical systems.

The appeal is that you don’t necessarily have to generate text strictly from left to right. You can potentially generate multiple tokens in parallel and refine a sequence using context on both sides. But that doesn’t automatically mean you get faster or better generation. You have to account for how many refinement steps you need, the computational cost of those steps, and the quality of the final result.

So I’m encouraged by the direction. What I’d want to look at closely is the comparison under similar training and inference budgets. We have a very mature autoregressive ecosystem, and diffusion is still exploring many of those design choices. There’s room for progress, but I wouldn’t call the outcome settled.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether diffusion models can become competitive and says the outcome is unsettled, but it does not say LLaDA remains substantially behind models available internally to Ermon’s team.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very exciting direction. Most of the progress in language modeling has focused on autoregressive models, and these efforts are asking a fundamental question: is that the only way to build a strong language model?

With diffusion, you can start with a partially masked sequence and iteratively refine it, using context from both directions. That gives you a different set of possibilities for generation, including filling in missing text and potentially generating multiple tokens in parallel.

But parallel generation doesn’t automatically mean faster generation, because you may need several rounds of refinement. So the important comparison is quality relative to the total compute and latency, as well as how effectively the models scale.

I see these efforts as encouraging evidence that the design space is broader than we’ve been exploring. There’s still a lot to establish, but having serious teams investigate alternatives is very valuable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses diffusion language models and says there is still much to establish, but it does not state that LLaDA’s models substantially trail models available internally to Ermon’s team.
